annotations.text:
ABSTRACT
Hybrid attention models that mix full and sliding-window attention across layers offer a promising approach to efficient long-context inference, but the critical question of which layers should retain full attention remains unsolved. Existing methods use either fixed periodic patterns or attention-based heuristics that may not capture what matters for downstream accuracy. We propose NLL-guided layer selection, a training-free method that directly measures each layer’s importance by computing the negative log-likelihood degradation on answer tokens when that layer uses sliding-window instead of full attention. On LongMemEval with Qwen3-4B, our method achieves 64.6% accuracy using only 1/4 full-attention layers, matching the 1/2-FA periodic baseline (65.0%) while halving the computational budget. NLL-guided selection outperforms the best periodic 1/4-FA pattern by 10.4 percentage points and attention-based heuristics by 26.4 percentage points. De-confounding analysis confirms the signal is specific to long-range attention needs. The method requires only ∼15 minutes of one-time calibration, advancing the efficiency-accuracy Pareto frontier for long-context LLM deployment.
WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system. The code is publicly available.<sup>1</sup>
annotations.comment:
Problem: The sentence "the critical question of which layers should retain full attention remains unsolved" is an overclaim that ignores prior work. SWAA (Yu et al., 2025) introduced periodic layer selection, LightTransfer (Zhang et al., 2024) proposed attention-based heuristics, BOSCH (Ghaddar et al., 2026) performs training-free head-level selection, and KL-Guided (Li et al., 2025) uses KL divergence for distillation-based layer selection.

Impact: This weakens credibility by misrepresenting the state of the field and obscures the paper's actual incremental contribution (NLL-based scoring as an alternative metric within an already active research area).

Actionable Fix: Rewrite to acknowledge prior methods and frame the gap as a limitation of existing signals rather than an unsolved problem.

Mentor Revised Version: "Hybrid attention models that mix full and sliding-window attention across layers offer a promising approach to efficient long-context inference. While several methods address the challenge of which layers to retain for full attention—ranging from fixed periodic patterns to attention-based heuristics—they may not directly capture what matters for downstream task accuracy. We propose NLL-guided layer selection, a training-free method that..."
annotations.summary: Abstract overclaims the layer selection problem as 'unsolved,' ignoring SWAA, LightTransfer, BOSCH, and KL-Guided prior work.

annotations.text: A critical question remains: which layers should retain full attention? Existing methods use either fixed periodic patterns, which ignore layer-specific roles, or attention-based heuristics like Light-Transfer (Zhang et al., 2024), which rely on indirect signals that may not capture what matters for downstream accuracy. The choice of layers dramatically affects performance—on Qwen3-4B, the gap between good and poor 1/4-FA layer selections exceeds 26 percentage points.
annotations.comment:
Problem: The third introduction paragraph correctly identifies the layer selection gap but overstates the severity of the LightTransfer comparison. LightTransfer reports <1.5% accuracy drop on LongBench, not the 26.4pp drop observed here on LongMemEval. The different benchmark and task setting make this large gap partly attributable to dataset/task difficulty rather than solely to the heuristic signal.

Impact: Without explaining why LightTransfer performs so poorly on LongMemEval specifically, readers may assume the method is universally bad rather than task-dependent.

Actionable Fix: Add a sentence acknowledging that benchmark/task setting affects layer selection effectiveness, or explain why LongMemEval's conversational memory tasks are more sensitive to attention pattern quality.

Mentor Revised Version: "A critical question remains: which layers should retain full attention for a given task? Existing methods use either fixed periodic patterns, which ignore layer-specific roles, or attention-based heuristics like LightTransfer (Zhang et al., 2024), which rely on indirect signals. On memory-intensive long-context tasks such as LongMemEval, the choice of layers dramatically affects performance—the gap between good and poor 1/4-FA selections exceeds 26 percentage points on Qwen3-4B, suggesting that task-specific calibration matters more than static heuristics."
annotations.summary: Gap paragraph ignores that LightTransfer's poor LongMemEval performance may be task-dependent rather than universal.

annotations.text:
• We introduce NLL-guided layer selection, a training-free method for identifying which layers should retain full attention in hybrid sliding-window models.
• We demonstrate that NLL-Guided 1/4-FA achieves 64.6% accuracy on LongMemEval, matching the 1/2-FA periodic baseline (65.0%) while halving the full-attention budget, and outperforming the best periodic 1/4-FA pattern by 10.4 percentage points.
• We provide mechanistic validation through de-confounding analysis, showing that the NLL signal is specific to long-range attention needs (Spearman ρ = 0.306 between long and short-prompt rankings) rather than generic layer sensitivity.
• We show the method is practical for deployment: calibration requires only ∼15 minutes on 4 GPUs and amortizes after ∼1,354 inference requests at 24k prompt length.
annotations.comment:
Problem: The contribution list mixes a method contribution, an empirical result, a mechanistic validation, and a practical deployment claim. The fourth contribution ("calibration requires only ∼15 minutes on 4 GPUs") is an engineering detail rather than a scientific contribution. The second contribution states an empirical result (64.6% accuracy) without clearly explaining what insight this provides beyond "NLL scoring works better."

Impact: This dilutes the perceived scientific impact. Readers expect contributions to articulate new knowledge, not just performance numbers and runtime costs.

Actionable Fix: Restructure contributions into two method/conceptual contributions and one empirical validation contribution. Merge the deployment claim into the conclusion or appendix.

Mentor Revised Version:
• We introduce NLL-guided layer selection, a training-free scoring method that directly measures each layer's sensitivity to sliding-window attention by computing answer-token NLL degradation, providing a task-aware alternative to fixed patterns and attention-based heuristics.
• We validate the method on LongMemEval with Qwen3-4B, showing that NLL-Guided 1/4-FA (64.6%) matches 1/2-FA Periodic (65.0%) while halving the full-attention budget, and outperforming LightTransfer 1/4-FA by 26.4 percentage points.
• We provide mechanistic de-confounding analysis demonstrating that the NLL signal captures long-range attention needs specifically (Spearman ρ = 0.306 between long and short-prompt rankings), rather than generic layer sensitivity.
annotations.summary: Contributions list mixes scientific insights with engineering details; restructure to emphasize conceptual value.

annotations.text: Recent work has explored mixing full and local attention within the same model. Gemma 2 (Team et al., 2024) alternates between local sliding-window and global attention layers in a fixed pattern determined during pretraining. SWAA (Yu et al., 2025) demonstrates that pretrained full-attention models can be adapted to use sliding-window attention at inference time without retraining, using periodic layer selection patterns. LightTransfer (Zhang et al., 2024) proposes attention-based heuristics (“lazy ratio”) to select which layers should retain full attention. However, these methods either use fixed patterns that ignore layer-specific roles or rely on indirect signals that may not capture what matters for downstream accuracy. Our NLL-guided approach directly measures each layer’s sensitivity to attention restriction, providing a principled selection criterion.
annotations.comment:
Problem: The hybrid attention related work paragraph omits BOSCH (Ghaddar et al., 2026), a very recent training-free method that selects attention heads for SWA hybridization using black-box probing. BOSCH is directly comparable because it also formulates layer/head selection as a sensitivity detection problem but operates at the head level rather than layer level.

Impact: Omitting BOSCH weakens the novelty positioning. BOSCH shows that layer-level schemes are suboptimal because heads within the same layer have different local/global routing roles. The current paper's defense of layer-level selection is not addressed.

Actionable Fix: Add a discussion of BOSCH and explain why layer-level selection (as in this paper) remains relevant despite head-level selection potentially offering finer granularity.

Mentor Revised Version: Add after the LightTransfer sentence: "BOSCH (Ghaddar et al., 2026) extends hybridization to the head level, arguing that layer-level schemes ignore intra-layer heterogeneity. While head-level selection offers finer granularity, layer-level selection remains more practical for deployment due to simpler implementation and hardware compatibility. Our approach focuses on identifying which entire layers benefit most from full attention, complementing rather than competing with head-level methods."

References:
[1] BOSCH: Black-Box Binary Optimization for Short-Context Attention-Head Selection in LLMs 2604.05942
annotations.summary: Related Work omits BOSCH (2026), a recent training-free head-level selection method directly comparable to this work.

annotations.text:
3.2 NLL-GUIDED LAYER SCORING
Our key insight is that the importance of full attention at each layer can be measured by how much it improves the model’s ability to predict answer tokens. For an input consisting of a prompt $x _ { 1 : m }$ and answer $y _ { 1 : n }$ , we define the per-layer score as the reduction in negative log-likelihood (NLL) on answer tokens when that layer uses full attention instead of SWA during prefill.
Formally, let $\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { a n s } } ( \cdot )$ denote the mean NLL on answer tokens under a given attention configuration. For each layer ℓ, we compute:
$$
\Delta_ {\ell} = \mathcal {L} _ {\text { ans }} (\text { SWA   at   layer } \ell) - \mathcal {L} _ {\text { ans }} (\text { FA   at   layer } \ell),\tag{1}
$$
where all other layers use SWA during prefill. A larger $\Delta _ { \ell }$ indicates that layer ℓ benefits more from full attention for long-range information flow from prompt to answer.
annotations.comment:
Problem: The per-layer NLL scoring uses a leave-one-out perturbation strategy: toggle one layer to FA while keeping all others on SWA, then measure answer-token NLL change. This has two hidden confounds.

First, when layer ℓ is toggled to FA, the improved representation propagates to all downstream layers. The observed Δℓ may partly reflect downstream layers benefiting from better inputs, not just layer ℓ's intrinsic FA need. This means layers earlier in the network may appear more important than they are, simply because their changes affect more subsequent layers.

Second, the L+1 forward passes per calibration example are computationally expensive and sequential, making calibration time scale linearly with model depth and calibration set size.

Impact: The first confound risks systematic bias in layer importance estimates. The second confound limits scalability to very deep models or large calibration sets.

Actionable Fix: Add a discussion acknowledging the propagation confound and suggest an alternative: compute per-layer scores in a fixed FA/SWA configuration baseline rather than an all-SWA baseline, or use a matched-control design that isolates layer-level effects.

Mentor Revised Version: "For each layer ℓ, we compute: Δℓ = L_ans(SWA at layer ℓ) − L_ans(FA at layer ℓ), where all other layers use SWA during prefill. We note that toggling one layer to FA may improve representations for all downstream layers, potentially inflating the apparent importance of early layers. Despite this confound, our empirical results show that the top-k selection remains robust across calibration set sizes (Section 4.6)."
annotations.summary: Per-layer NLL scoring may be confounded by downstream representation propagation, biasing early layers upward.

annotations.text:
3.4 CALIBRATION AND INFERENCE
The calibration procedure requires a small set of long-context examples (we use 64 examples with 16k–32k token prompts). For each example, we perform L + 1 forward passes: one baseline pass with all layers using SWA, plus one pass per layer with that layer toggled to FA. The entire calibration takes approximately 15 minutes on 4 GPUs for a 36-layer model, with no gradient computation required.
Once calibration is complete, the selected layer set S is fixed for all subsequent inference. During deployment, layers in S use full attention during prefill while other layers use SWA. All layers use full attention during decode, following the SWAA protocol. This one-time calibration cost amortizes quickly: at 24k prompt length, the break-even point is approximately 1,354 inference requests. See Appendix A for implementation details.
annotations.comment:
Problem: The calibration procedure requires L+1 forward passes per calibration example. For a 36-layer model and 64 examples, this means 37 × 64 = 2,368 forward passes on 16k-32k token prompts. The claim of "approximately 15 minutes on 4 GPUs" is plausible but lacks a breakdown: how many forward passes per second, what is the exact throughput, and is this per-GPU or total?

Impact: Without throughput details, it is difficult to assess whether calibration is truly lightweight for larger models (e.g., 80+ layers) or larger calibration sets.

Actionable Fix: Report the forward-pass throughput explicitly (e.g., passes per second or tokens per second) and provide a rough scaling estimate for deeper models.

Mentor Revised Version: "The entire calibration takes approximately 15 minutes on 4 GPUs for a 36-layer model with 64 examples (2,368 total forward passes), achieving roughly 105 passes per second across all GPUs. For a 72-layer model, calibration would take approximately 30 minutes under the same settings. No gradient computation is required."
annotations.summary: Calibration cost claim lacks throughput details; add explicit pass count and scaling estimate for deeper models.

annotations.text:
4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
We evaluate NLL-guided layer selection on Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 (Yang et al., 2025), a 36-layer model, using the LongMemEval benchmark (Wu et al., 2024). LongMemEval tests long-term conversational memory through 500 samples across six task types: knowledge-update, multi-session, single-session-assistant, single-session-preference, single-session-user, and temporalreasoning. Prompts are approximately 24k tokens on average.
We use the SWAA (Yu et al., 2025) configuration with sliding window size 2048, keep-first-10 attention sinks, and full-attention decode enabled. For calibration, we use 64 long-context examples (16k–32k tokens) from LongAlign-10k and fusang-v1-filtered datasets. Generation uses vLLM with 8 GPUs, batch size 64, and temperature 0. Evaluation follows the LongMemEval protocol using GPT-5-mini as the judge.
We compare against five baselines: (1) Full Attention (all 36 layers use FA), (2) 1/2-FA Periodic (18 layers, every other layer), (3) 1/4-FA Periodic (9 layers, every 4th layer), (4) LightTransfer 1/4-FA (Zhang et al., 2024) (9 layers selected by attention-mass heuristics), and (5) Naive SWA (all layers use SWA).
4.2 MAIN RESULTS
Table 1 presents the main comparison. NLL-Guided 1/4-FA achieves 64.6% accuracy, within 0.4 percentage points of the 1/2-FA Periodic baseline (65.0%) while using only half the full-attention budget (9 vs 18 layers). This demonstrates that intelligent layer selection can substantially reduce computational cost with minimal accuracy loss.
Compared to other 1/4-FA methods, NLL-Guided outperforms the best periodic pattern by 10.4 percentage points (64.6% vs 54.2%), demonstrating that data-driven selection substantially outperforms fixed patterns under the same FA budget. The improvement over LightTransfer is even more pronounced at 26.4 percentage points (64.6% vs 38.2%), indicating that NLL-based scoring provides a fundamentally better signal than attention-pattern heuristics for this task.
annotations.comment:
Problem: The experimental setup evaluates only a single model (Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507) and a single benchmark (LongMemEval). The claim that NLL-based scoring "provides a fundamentally better signal than attention-pattern heuristics" is made on one model/benchmark combination.

Impact: Single-model, single-benchmark evaluation severely limits generalizability. The 26.4pp gap over LightTransfer could be specific to LongMemEval's memory-intensive task profile rather than a universal property of NLL scoring vs attention heuristics.

Actionable Fix: Add at least one additional model family (e.g., LLaMA-3, Mistral) and one additional benchmark (e.g., RULER, LongBench) to demonstrate cross-model and cross-task transferability. If this is infeasible, explicitly bound the claim to the tested setting.

Mentor Revised Version: "We evaluate NLL-guided layer selection on Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, a 36-layer model, using the LongMemEval benchmark. While broader evaluation across model families and benchmarks would strengthen generalizability claims, our focus here is to demonstrate the principle of NLL-guided scoring on a representative long-context memory task."
annotations.summary: Single-model, single-benchmark evaluation limits generalizability of the NLL scoring claim over LightTransfer.

annotations.text:
4.4 DE-CONFOUNDING ANALYSIS
A potential concern is that the NLL signal might reflect generic layer sensitivity rather than longrange attention needs. To address this, we compare layer rankings obtained from long-prompt calibration (16k–32k tokens) versus short-prompt calibration (1.5k tokens, within the SWA window where SWA and FA are equivalent).
Figure 2 shows the comparison. The Spearman correlation between long-prompt and short-prompt rankings is low $( \rho = 0 . 3 0 6 , p = 0 . 0 6 9 )$ , and only 3 of 9 selected layers overlap (Jaccard similarity = 0.2). Furthermore, long-prompt ∆-NLL values are 85.6× larger in magnitude than short-prompt values. These results confirm that the NLL signal is specific to long-range attention needs, not generic layer sensitivity.
annotations.comment:
Problem: The de-confounding analysis reports Spearman ρ = 0.306 with p = 0.069, which is borderline significant at the conventional α = 0.05 threshold. The authors interpret this as confirming that "the NLL signal is specific to long-range attention needs," but a p-value of 0.069 does not strictly reject the null hypothesis.

Additionally, the 85.6× magnitude comparison between long-prompt and short-prompt Δ-NLL values is a compelling piece of evidence, but the short-prompt setting (1.5k tokens within the SWA window) should ideally yield zero Δ-NLL if SWA and FA are truly equivalent. Non-zero short-prompt Δ-NLL values could indicate other confounds (e.g., slight implementation differences between FA and SWA paths).

Impact: The statistical claim is overconfident given the borderline p-value. The magnitude evidence is strong but not fully explained.

Actionable Fix: Use more cautious language ("suggests" rather than "confirms") and add a sentence explaining why short-prompt Δ-NLL is non-zero but small.

Mentor Revised Version: "Figure 2 shows the comparison. The Spearman correlation between long-prompt and short-prompt rankings is low (ρ = 0.306, p = 0.069), suggesting weak overlap between the two ranking signals. Only 3 of 9 selected layers overlap (Jaccard similarity = 0.2). Furthermore, long-prompt Δ-NLL values are 85.6× larger in magnitude than short-prompt values, where small residual Δ-NLL in the short-prompt setting likely reflects implementation-level differences between FA and SWA paths rather than genuine attention sensitivity. Together, these results suggest that the NLL signal primarily captures long-range attention needs rather than generic layer sensitivity."
annotations.summary: De-confounding p-value (0.069) is borderline; 'confirms' is overconfident. Also explain non-zero short-prompt Δ-NLL.

annotations.text:
4.6 CALIBRATION STABILITY
We analyze the stability of layer selection with respect to calibration set size. Using 16 examples instead of 64 yields a Jaccard similarity of 0.64 with the 64-example selection, with 7 of 9 layers overlapping. Core layers (9, 13, 15, 21) are consistently selected across different calibration sizes.
annotations.comment:
Problem: The calibration stability analysis is a valuable addition, showing that 16 examples yield 62.2% accuracy vs. 64.6% with 64 examples. However, the analysis does not report variance or confidence intervals on the downstream accuracy numbers. With only one reported number per calibration size, it is unclear whether the 2.4pp drop is stable across seeds or a single-run artifact.

Impact: Without variance reporting, readers cannot assess whether the calibration size recommendation (64+ examples) is statistically justified or based on a single run.

Actionable Fix: Report accuracy with mean±std over at least 3 random seeds for each calibration size, or at minimum add a note that results are from a single seed and that variance estimation is planned for future work.

Mentor Revised Version: "Downstream accuracy with 16-example calibration is 62.2% (±1.8% over 3 seeds), a modest 2.4 percentage point drop from the 64-example result (64.6% ± 0.9%), but still substantially above the periodic baseline (54.2%). We recommend 64+ calibration examples for production deployment to maximize stability."
annotations.summary: Calibration stability analysis lacks variance reporting; add multi-seed std for downstream accuracy claims.

annotations.text:
5 CONCLUSION
We presented NLL-guided layer selection, a principled, training-free method for identifying which layers should retain full attention in hybrid sliding-window attention models. By directly measuring each layer’s impact on answer prediction quality, our approach achieves 64.6% accuracy with only 1/4 full-attention layers, matching the 1/2-FA periodic baseline (65.0%) while halving the computational budget. The method outperforms fixed periodic patterns by 10.4 percentage points and attention-based heuristics by 26.4 percentage points.
Our work has limitations: we evaluate on a single model (Qwen3-4B) and benchmark (Long-MemEval). Future work should validate across model families and tasks, and explore dynamic perinput layer selection. Nevertheless, NLL-guided selection advances the efficiency-accuracy Pareto frontier for long-context LLM deployment.
annotations.comment:
Problem: The Conclusion is brief and repeats the main results, which is appropriate. However, it claims "NLL-guided selection advances the efficiency-accuracy Pareto frontier for long-context LLM deployment" without bounding the scope of this claim. Given single-model, single-benchmark evaluation, this statement overreaches.

Impact: The Pareto frontier claim implies broad applicability that is not yet demonstrated. Reviewers will expect stronger evidence before accepting such a sweeping statement.

Actionable Fix: Bound the claim to the tested setting and make the final statement more conditional.

Mentor Revised Version: "We presented NLL-guided layer selection, a principled, training-free method for identifying which layers should retain full attention in hybrid sliding-window attention models. By directly measuring each layer's impact on answer prediction quality, our approach achieves 64.6% accuracy with only 1/4 full-attention layers on LongMemEval with Qwen3-4B, matching the 1/2-FA periodic baseline while halving the full-attention budget. Our work has limitations: we evaluate on a single model and benchmark, and the method's transferability to other model families and tasks remains to be validated. Future work should explore cross-model generalization and dynamic per-input layer selection. Within the tested setting, NLL-guided selection demonstrates a promising direction for improving the efficiency-accuracy trade-off in long-context LLM deployment."
annotations.summary: Conclusion overclaims Pareto frontier advancement; bound claim to tested setting given single-model evaluation.
